<reason>Both sides were sharp, closed-book-disciplined, and well-structured, with clean Q/A formatting. CON built an elegant central dilemma: if quotas have teeth they collapse into a solidarity fund (its own alternative); if they lack teeth they repeat 2015. That was the most original move in the debate. But PRO neutralized it twice over: first by reframing the buy-out as "an obligation with two ways of discharging it," where the payment is only owed because a share was allocated, and then by the memorable comparative — "delete the quota and the money is charity, arriving late, negotiated boat by boat; keep the quota and the money is a debt." That directly answers the dissolution trap rather than dodging it. PRO also anchored the clash to the motion's actual wording better: CON's capacity-and-funding alternative, by its own admission, leaves the frontline registering, adjudicating and hosting most arrivals, i.e. exactly the arrangement the motion rejects — "a better-equipped Lesbos." CON's reply to PRO's decisive pressure question (who hosts the recognised refugees?) was its weakest moment: it redefined the burden as throughput only and leaned on an overstated claim that recognised refugees "can move lawfully under existing mobility rules," which does more asserting than answering. Similarly, CON's secondary-movement attack was blunted when PRO showed that matched allocation still changes who registers, who funds, and who is legally responsible, even if destinations look similar. CON's backlash and enforcement-realism points remain partly live, and PRO conceded some states will buy out, so this is competitive rather than lopsided — but PRO made the decisive comparison easier to grasp and dealt with pressure more directly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's handling of CON's dissolution dilemma: rather than deny that a quota can be discharged by payment, PRO accepted it and reframed — a quota with a buy-out is an obligation with two modes of performance, and the payment exists only because a share was allocated; strip the quota and the same money becomes ad hoc charity. Paired with the pressure question "who hosts the recognised refugees?", which forced CON into conceding permanent frontline hosting, this converted CON's cleverest argument into PRO's framing of the motion.</best_rebuttal>
